entities.name: Kushan Empire
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Kushan Empire (c. 30-375 CE) was a major Central Asian empire that at its height controlled territory spanning modern Afghanistan, Pakistan, northern India, and parts of China's Xinjiang, creating a crossroads civilization that was the pivot point for the exchange of Buddhism, art, trade, and ideas between Rome, Persia, India, and China. The Kushans created the first iconographic representations of the Buddha in human form — previously Buddha was represented only by symbols — establishing the Gandharan art style that became the foundation of Buddhist visual culture worldwide.

The Kushans were originally a Yuezhi people displaced from Central Asia by the Xiongnu, who migrated through Bactria to create a prosperous trading empire along the Silk Road. Kanishka the Great (r. c. 127-163 CE), the dynasty's greatest ruler, convened the Fourth Buddhist Council, sponsored the translation of Buddhist texts into Sanskrit, patronized the arts that created Gandharan Buddhist sculpture, and was personally connected to the spread of Mahayana Buddhism.

Kushan territory along the Silk Road meant it was simultaneously exposed to Roman, Persian, Indian, and Chinese influences: Kushan coins showed Greek gods, Indian deities, Zoroastrian figures, and Buddha — sometimes on the same coin series. The empire declined from the 3rd century CE under Sasanian Persian pressure, fragmenting into local kingdoms, but the Gandharan art tradition it created spread Buddhist iconography across Central and East Asia.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Kushan Empire created the first images of the Buddha in human form — establishing the visual vocabulary of Buddhist art used across Asia for 2,000 years — making it the most consequential empire in the history of Buddhist civilization.
